I am 37 years old and have farmed these fields in Quzhou since I was a girl. I only finished primary school, but I know this land better than any book. Here on the North China Plain, our soil is thick and fertile, but the seasons are tight. My family has about 6 mu of land, and I will plant it the way my parents and neighbors always have — winter wheat followed by summer corn. That is the only rotation I trust to feed my family and leave grain to sell.

This autumn, I will sow improved wheat seed on all 6 mu. I buy my seed and fertilizer from the county supply store. Before sowing, I will run the rotary tiller to break up the soil and mix in the base fertilizer. I will irrigate four times: once before winter so the seedlings don't dry out, once at green-up in March, once at jointing when the stems shoot up, and once during grain filling. I will spray twice — herbicide after sowing, and another round later if I see aphids or rust. In early June, when the wheat turns golden, I will harvest it quickly.

There is no time to rest. Within days, I must plant summer corn, or the growing season will be too short before autumn cold arrives. I will use hybrid corn seed because it grows fast and yields heavy ears. I will drill the corn directly into the wheat stubble with almost no tillage — there is no time to plough, and the stubble helps keep moisture. I will side-dress nitrogen when the corn reaches knee height, and irrigate three times through the hot summer. I will spray for weeds and corn borers. By late September, I will harvest the corn and then prepare the land again for next year's wheat.

I do not grow vegetables or other crops on my main land because I do not have the skill to sell them, and one bad market price could ruin us. Wheat and corn have stable buyers at the village collection point. This is what I know, and this is what I will do.
